newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST--Creeping U.S. PPI seen only minor threat.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST--Creeping U.S. PPI seen only minor threat.

text.p: Wholesale price inflation remains well under control despite a recent boost in energy prices, analysts said.

With the U.S. economy apparently undergoing at least a mild deceleration, modest increases in upcoming producer price index (PPI) data will not likely push the Federal Reserve closer to a short-term interest rate hike, economists said.
"Overall, we see the inflation picture as remaining quite benign," said Peter Kretzmer, senior economist at NationsBanc Capital Markets Inc.
The Bureau of Labor Statistics will offer economists fresh inflation numbers to crunch on Friday, October 11, when it releases the September PPI report at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT.
The consensus forecast of a Reuters poll is a monthly rise of 0.3 percent in PPI, with a gain of 0.2 percent in the core rate which excludes volatile food and energy prices.
That would indicate a modest rebound from a core rate decline of 0.1 percent in August, but analysts played down the chances of any sustained surge in wholesale prices.
"I don't think there's anything in PPI to give the Fed cause for worry," said William Griggs, managing director at consulting firm Griggs and Santow Inc.
"The current data argue that the economy is slowing down and the price picture isn't getting much worse," he added.
Oil prices have risen nearly 50 percent from a year ago amid mounting Middle East tension and heating oil prices have surged to their highest point since the 1991 Gulf War.
Over time, higher energy prices will push overall inflation higher, analysts noted.
"Nobody seems to mention this, but that will creep into PPI," said Mitchell Held, chief economist at Smith Barney.
Of greater concern for Fed inflation-fighters are the increasing reports of labor market tightness and steady growth in U.S. wages, analysts said.
"There's a good chance the Fed will tighten at the November (13) Federal Open Market Committee meeting, more on higher labor costs than anything else," Held said.
But wholesale price pressures create less concern. Weak demand-side pressures prevent manufacturers from transferring raw materials price increases to customers, analysts said.
"We really don't see any of the classic inflation where businesses have the power to pass on price increases," Kretzmer said.
Crude and intermediate wholesale prices have actually declined over the last 12 months, helping squash fears of faster overall PPI, analysts said.
Crude goods prices are down 12.4 percent and intermediate goods prices have fallen 1.8 percent since last August.
Still, some analysts see an increase in core PPI toward an annualized 2.0 to 3.0 percent rate in coming months from a mild 1.4 percent over the 12 months ending in August.

"That's not particularly strong, but the Fed is going to want to guard against acceleration at some point," said Held, adding that he expects the Fed to boost the federal funds rate by a half- or quarter-point from 5.25 percent by yearend.

But a slowing economy, with some estimates for sub-2.0 percent gross domestic product in the third and fourth quarters, down from 4.7 percent in the second quarter, should minimize the inflation risks, analysts said.
"It's not that there isn't any price pressure," Griggs said. "But there's not a great deal."
